fixes.explanation: Right, he stays. Jacob finishes the week's celebration, and Laban gives him Rachel as his wife (Genesis 29:28). Then the text says Jacob worked for Laban another seven years (Genesis 29:30). Nobody packs a bag in this passage, friend.

Payment never comes up at this well, friend. The text says the shepherds roll the stone away once all the flocks have been gathered, then water the sheep (Genesis 29:3). No fee in sight. Just a big stone and a lot of waiting.

They know him. When Jacob asks if they know Laban the grandson of Nahor, they answer, “We know him…” (Genesis 29:5). Then Jacob asks if Laban is well, and they say, “Yes,” and add that his daughter Rachel is coming with his sheep (Genesis 29:6). Jacob asked about one man, and the shepherds had news about him right away.

He sure does. As soon as Jacob sees Rachel with Laban's sheep, he goes up, rolls the stone away from the mouth of the well, and waters his uncle's sheep (Genesis 29:10). Just before this, the shepherds told him, “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away…” (Genesis 29:8). Then Jacob walks up and rolls it himself. That tells me he was glad to see Rachel.

It's true, he does it himself. The text says that as soon as Jacob saw Rachel with Laban's sheep, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well (Genesis 29:10). Then he watered his uncle's sheep. Whew. I'd want a nap after moving that stone.

Nope, no waiting by the well in this story, friend. Once Jacob tells her he's Rebekah's son, the text says she ran and told her father (Genesis 29:12). Ran! If somebody told me a long-lost relative was standing at the well, I'd be moving too. I'd trip over my own apron, but I'd be moving.

Duties sound like a job description, but that's not what Laban asks for. He says, "Tell me what your wages should be." (Genesis 29:15) He wants Jacob to name his pay. I've been paid in a 25 cent price sticker, so I know a wage when I see one.

Right, Rachel is the younger one. Laban's older daughter is Leah, and the younger is Rachel (Genesis 29:16). Leah first, Rachel second. Write it on your oven mitt, friend, because that order is about to matter.

Five is a nice round number, but it's not Jacob's. He says, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." (Genesis 29:18) Seven. That's a lot of batches, friend, and the text says he made the offer because he loves her.

That's Laban's reply. He says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) So when Jacob offers seven years for Rachel, that's what Laban says back. He tells Jacob to stay.

Isaac doesn't come up in Laban's reply. He says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) No asking Dad first here, friend. Laban's words are all about Jacob staying.

Isaac's flocks never come up here, friend. Laban says they will give Jacob the younger one in return for another seven years of work (Genesis 29:27). What Laban asks for is Jacob's work, seven more years of it.
